id.description: The interaction, as it arrived in the app's `mcp_login_url`. Not a credential: it names a pending request the server already holds, and approving it needs the app user's own access token.

app_id.description: The app this authorization is for. The approving token's `app_id` must match it — an interaction of one app cannot be approved with a session from another.

client_name.description: What the MCP client calls itself, or `null` if it named nothing. **Unverified** — see `client_name_verified`.

client_name_verified.description: Always `false`. The client named itself — in an unauthenticated dynamic registration or in its own Client ID Metadata Document — so the name must be rendered as a claim and never as an identity. Only `client_id_host` was checked, by fetching the document from it. There is no verified case, which is why this is a literal and not a boolean: a `true` branch would be dead code that looked like a safeguard.

client_id_host.description: The hostname of the client's `client_id` when that id is the HTTPS URL of a Client ID Metadata Document, which the authorization server fetched from this host; `null` for a client that registered itself by dynamic registration. Show it beside the name: it is the one part of the client's description somebody checked.

redirect_uri_host.description: The hostname of the redirect URI this authorization will answer to — where the authorization code is sent. Show it on the consent screen (MCP 2026-07-28 requires it). An IPv6 literal keeps its brackets.

redirect_uri_loopback.description: `true` when the redirect URI is `http` on a loopback address (`localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `[::1]`): the answer goes to a program on the person's own computer, on any port it chose. Warn about it, for example: "This client receives the answer on this computer (127.0.0.1). Approve only if you started it here."

scopes.description: The scopes the client asked for, to show the person before they approve.

already_granted.description: Whether this user has already approved this client. It is a record of what they answered last time, and **this route makes no second use of it**: an app that skips its own consent screen when this is `true` is the only thing deciding that, and approve succeeds identically for a user who holds no grant at all. The standing grant is read elsewhere, on every request to the app's MCP endpoint. Withdrawing it is `DELETE /api/client/mcp/grants/:clientId` for the person themselves and `DELETE /api/apps/:id/users/:userId/mcp-grants/:clientId` for the developer. A withdrawal makes this `false` again at the next authorization **and stops the client at its very next MCP call**, unexpired access token and all — up to fifteen minutes of it — because the endpoint keys that check on the `client_id` the token carries.

expires_at.description: When the interaction stops being approvable. Ten minutes from the authorize step; afterwards both approve and deny answer `interaction_expired`.
